s1: The story starts at IBM in the early 1990s with two research efforts. At the Watson Lab, Vesta explored how parallel programs could partition files across disks. At all Madden in California, Tiger Shark was built for something that sounds unrelated, streaming multimedia. But video means many steady streams, served from an array of disks. So you stripe everything and never let one disk become the hot spot. That's exactly what a scientific code writing a checkpoint wants too. The two lineages merged into GPFS around 1998 with a standard Unix interface, so ordinary programs just worked. The foundational document is a 2002 paper at the FAST conference from two all Madden researchers. Its three big ideas, shared disks, wide striping and distributed locking are still the skeleton of the system. It describes ASCI-Y, a 512 node machine with 140 terabytes of disk, where 16 nodes could drive the machine's entire 12 gigabytes per second of I-O bandwidth. Hold on to those numbers. We'll compare them with a modern system later. Since then, Spectrum Scale in 2015, when IBM put that prefix on its storage products, and storage scale in early 2023 when the prefix was dropped. Same lineage, same core design.
s4: Here's the problem everything else is built around. POSIX promises that if one process writes and another then reads, the reader sees the right, even across machines. GPFS keeps that promise across the whole cluster. The paper's phrase is single node equivalent semantics. How? Without asking a central server for permission on every operation. The answer is tokens. A token is a permission slip. This node may cache and operate on this object in this way. The token manager hands them out and each node's local lock manager makes fine-grained decisions with no network round trip for as long as the node holds the right token. For file data, tokens are byte ranges. The first node to write a file gets a token for the entire file. If nobody else shows up, it never talks to the token manager again. Now a second node wants to write the back half. The first node is asked to give up part of its range, the range splits, and now both write in parallel with no further coordination. Notice that the ranges get rounded to block boundaries. That's deliberate and it's why alignment matters. If two nodes write different bytes inside the same block, they need the same token, and the token, along with the dirty data, ping pongs between them. The node has a similar problem. Every writer changes the file's size and modification time, and if each updated the node on disk, it would be a stampede. So GPS selects a met node for each open file. Writers send a node changes to it, and it alone reads and writes that a node on disk. For truly fine-grained sharing, the paper also describes data shipping, where each block has an owner and everyone else sends their I-O to it. You can see all of this in a benchmark. On Summit's file system, the I-O 500 test with 504 nodes has an easy mode where every process writes its own file and a hard mode where all of them write small, unaligned, interleaved chunks into one shared file. Easy, about two terabytes per second. Hard, about half a gigabyte per second. A factor of roughly 3,800 on identical hardware. The slide doesn't break down why, but the cost of sharing blocks, token traffic and partial block read modify write is the usual suspect. Reads are far more forgiving, about 65 times slower instead of 3,800.
s7: Let's zoom out to what a real deployment looks like. The common HPC shape has three tiers. On the left, hundreds or thousands of compute nodes running the scale client. In the middle, a fast fabric, infiniband or ethernet. On the right, a set of building blocks, servers with storage behind them. Inside the file system, you carve storage into pools. Typically a fast pool for metadata and larger, cheaper pools for data. A policy engine which scans and nodes in parallel, places new files in the right pool, and migrates or deletes old ones based on attributes like age, size or owner. File sets carve the namespace into subtrees with their own quotas, and independent file sets can have their own in-node space. Failure groups tell the system which disks share a fate, a power supply, an enclosure, a rack, so two replicas land in different groups. Clusters can reach beyond themselves too. Remote cluster mounts let one cluster mount a file system owned by another, and an FM, Active File Management, caches data asynchronously between sites for disaster recovery or data sharing. There's even a shared nothing flavor, file placement optimizer, released in 2012, where each node's local disks contribute to the pool. And a software-only addition, Erasure Code Edition, that runs the declustered raid on ordinary servers. The biggest example I can verify from public sources is Alpine Oak Ridge's file system for the Summit Supercomputer. 250 petabytes, served by 154 NSD servers on 100 gigabit in Finneband, with a 16 megabyte block size. Its peak is about 2.5 terabytes per second sequential, and 2.2 random. Compare that with ASCI-White. Capacity is about 1,800 times bigger, bandwidth about 200 times, so reading the entire file system once took ASCI-White about three hours and would take Alpine about 28. Capacity has outrun bandwidth, a basic fact of HPC storage and a big reason tiers and policies exist. It's a rough comparison since machines, years, and measurements differ, but the direction is the point.
